questions.question: What's wrong with this?
options: Without `override` (and `virtual` on the base), this HIDES Animal's Speak instead of overriding it — polymorphism won't apply
Dog can't have a method named Speak
questions.explanation: Without `virtual` in the base and `override` here, this is a completely separate method that happens to share a name. Called through an `Animal`-typed reference, Animal's original Speak (or a compiler warning about hiding) applies, not Dog's — polymorphism breaks silently.

questions.question: Given `public class Animal { public Animal(string name) { ... } }`, what must `public class Dog : Animal` do?
options: Nothing special — Dog automatically gets a parameterless constructor
Dog's constructor(s) must call `: base(name)` with a matching argument, since Animal has no parameterless constructor
Dog cannot inherit from Animal in this case
Dog must redeclare the `name` field itself
questions.explanation: Since Animal only defines a constructor that takes a `string name`, there's no free parameterless one. Every Dog constructor must explicitly call `base(name)` (or another Animal constructor) to properly construct the inherited part.

questions.question: What does `protected` allow that `private` does not?
options: Access from anywhere in the same project
Access from classes that inherit from this one
Access from any class in any project
questions.explanation: `protected` members are visible to the declaring class AND any class that inherits from it, while remaining hidden from unrelated outside code. `private` is visible only inside the exact declaring class.

questions.explanation: This is exactly the polymorphism pattern: a `List<Animal>` can hold any Animal subtype, and each call to the virtual `Speak()` runs the ACTUAL object's override — Dog's, then Cat's.

questions.question: `base.Speak()` inside an override calls the derived class's own version again (infinite recursion).
questions.explanation: `base.Speak()` explicitly calls the BASE class's implementation, skipping the override. It's how you extend behavior rather than fully replacing it, with no recursion.
